analysis.one_liner: Let victims sue over racial discrimination in economic life, even without intent, and barred forced arbitration of such claims.
analysis.headline: Referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended, with support from 4 of 100 senators.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten a post-Civil War civil rights law (42 U.S.C. 1981) to cover racial discrimination in economic life — getting a loan, buying insurance, shopping, renting, hiring, or contracting — even when the discrimination is not intentional but shows up in results (disparate impact). It would have made it much easier to sue, by lowering the proof standard, letting anyone harmed sue even without a contract with the defendant, guaranteeing a jury trial, and voiding forced-arbitration clauses for these claims. It was written in response to Supreme Court decisions, especially Comcast v. National Association of African American-Owned Media in 2020, that Congress said had weakened these protections.
analysis.who_benefits: People of color who face discrimination in everyday economic life — being denied credit or insurance, refused service by a store or online platform, steered to worse terms in housing or contracting, or burdened by pollution. Under current law they often cannot win unless they prove the decision was made because of their race; the bill would have let them win by showing race was one motivating factor or that a facially neutral policy has a discriminatory effect they can prove, and it would have guaranteed them a jury rather than a private arbitrator.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People facing racial discrimination in economic life

how_it_helps.text: Makes a practice with a discriminatory effect (disparate impact) illegal across economic activity — credit, insurance, shopping, employment contracting, and property — even without proof of intentional discrimination; the user of the practice must prove a substantial business necessity to justify it.

Lowers the burden of proof: intentional discrimination is shown when race was a motivating factor, instead of the current requirement that the harm would not have occurred but for the discrimination — a direct response to the Supreme Court's 2020 Comcast decision.

Opens the courthouse door: anyone actually injured can sue, not only people who had a contract with the defendant, and employers' and governments' responsibility for their agents' and employees' conduct is spelled out.
Guarantees a jury trial and makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for these claims, so a company cannot force a discrimination claim into a private arbitration process.
Gives plaintiffs a four-year window to sue instead of shorter state deadlines, and the new rules would have applied to claims already pending when the bill became law.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that would face suits under the new standard: banks and other lenders, insurers, retailers, landlords, employers, and online platforms, through litigation, settlement, and the cost of auditing neutral practices (like credit scoring or pricing formulas) for discriminatory effects. Arbitration providers and the practice of forced arbitration also lose, since these claims could no longer be routed there. Some of those costs would likely be passed to customers in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders, insurers, retailers, and online platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill applied retroactively to claims already pending, changing the rules in the middle of existing lawsuits — the kind of retroactive change courts and defendants often challenge as unfair.

The definitions are extremely broad ('economic activity' has 'the broadest meaning permissible under the Constitution') and any person harmed — not just a contracting party — could sue, which could expose businesses to costly litigation over neutral policies like credit scores, insurance pricing, or security practices even where no one intended discrimination.

A disparate-impact standard pressures organizations to redesign or abandon facially neutral criteria (in lending, insurance, or policing of online commerce) that are genuinely useful, because any practice with a discriminatory effect must be proven a 'substantial business necessity' or be replaced.

Banning pre-dispute arbitration removes a forum that can be faster and cheaper for an individual claimant than a jury case, though it also strips the class-action and court protections that make civil rights suits effective.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a borrower, shopper, or renter who was treated differently because of race, current law is a steep climb: prove intent, be a party to a contract, survive a motion to compel arbitration. The bill would have removed each obstacle, which is a real, concrete gain for ordinary people. The costs are real too — broad liability exposure for lenders, insurers, retailers, and platforms, litigation over neutral business criteria, and retroactive application to pending cases — and a more carefully drawn bill might have phased in the rules and limited standing. On balance the bill's design favors plaintiffs heavily, but its core purpose was to restore protections the Supreme Court had narrowed, and it never advanced far enough for any of these trade-offs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, with Cory Booker and Ron Wyden listed as original cosponsors, framing it as a response to Supreme Court decisions — Comcast Corp. v. NAAOM (2020) and General Building Contractors Ass'n v. Pennsylvania (1982) — that Congress found had 'weakened the scope and effectiveness' of federal civil rights protections.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the same day, June 24, 2021.

No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action. The bill's action history ends with the committee referral, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Total support never grew beyond the sponsor and 3 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 100 senators; no Republican ever signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses in lending, insurance, retail, and online commerce are better off, since they avoid a new disparate-impact lawsuit pathway and keep their mandatory arbitration clauses; the narrower Supreme Court standards in Comcast v. NAAOM remain the law.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as restoring civil rights protections narrowed by the Supreme Court

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat without action from its referral in June 2021 until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only supporters were 4 Democratic senators, no Republican cosponsored, and opposition consisted of inaction rather than a recorded position.

industries.note: Granting or denying credit is explicitly covered, so underwriting criteria with a discriminatory effect would have to be proven a substantial business necessity or changed. Lenders would face suits from rejected applicants who need not have had a contract with them.

The bill expressly covers access to insurance, so pricing and underwriting formulas could be challenged for discriminatory effects and insurers could be sued by anyone actually injured, not just policyholders.

Serving or refusing to serve a customer — in person or online — falls within the bill's definition of economic activity, and standing extends beyond contract parties, broadening exposure for refusal-of-service and marketplace-suspension disputes.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the forced-arbitration system
industries.note: Pre-dispute arbitration agreements would be unenforceable for these claims, moving a stream of disputes out of private arbitration and into public courts with jury trials.
New and easier claims, a guaranteed jury, a four-year window, and broad standing would expand the market for civil rights litigation.
